## Abstract

Objective

Non-healing diabetic foot ulcers are a leading cause of disability and death in diabetic patients, which

often results in lower limb amputation. This study aimed to investigate the impact of biomarkers on the

healing of diabetic foot ulcers by utilizing dynamic serum proteomics and skin proteomic analysis,

combined with clinical case follow-up studies.

Methods

To analyze dynamic serum proteomic changes in four groups, age-matched normal subjects, diabetic

patients, pre-treatment diabetic foot ulcer patients, and healed diabetic foot ulcer patients were selected.

The differential proteins were screened in conjunction with normal and diabetic foot ulcer skin

proteomics. In this study, a total of 80 patients with diabetic foot ulcers were enrolled and monitored for

3–6 months during treatment. To verify the significance of the differential proteins, age-matched diabetic

patients (240 patients) and healthy controls (160 patients) were included as controls.

Results

Dynamic serum proteomics trend showed that the level of negative regulatory proteins related to endothelial cell migration, angiogenesis, and vascular development was significantly decreased after

treatment of diabetic foot ulcer. This study also found that there is an opposite trend of differential protein biological processes, which is mainly enriched in protein activation cascade, immunoglobulin

production, and complement activation. The researchers identified the core proteins APOA1, LPA, and APOA2 through a convergence of serum and skin proteomics screening. Clinical cases further validated

that APOA1 levels are decreased in diabetic foot ulcer patients and are correlated with disease severity.

Conclusions

Based on our dynamic proteomics and clinical case studies, our bioinformatic analysis suggests that

APOA1 plays a critical role in linking coagulation, inflammation, angiogenesis, and wound repair, making it a key protein that promotes the healing of diabetic foot ulcers.

## Introduction

Diabetic foot ulcers (DFU) and amputations are among the most feared complications of diabetes [1].

Impaired wound healing is a significant clinical challenge [2] and the primary cause of disability and mortality in diabetic patients with lower extremity amputation [3]. Despite advances in treatments,

including wound debridement, off-loading, medication, wound dressings, and infection prevention through ulcer cleanliness [4], non-healing DFU remains a serious clinical issue [5]. The formation of

granulation tissue and angiogenesis are closely linked to wound healing [6]. However, chronic inflammation and reduced angiogenesis in a hyperglycemic environment can disrupt the normal healing


<!-- Page 3 -->


Page 3/27

process, resulting in DFU that do not heal properly [7]. Various factors contribute to this problem, such as insufficient angiogenesis, excessive oxidative stress, an exaggerated inflammatory response, peripheral

neuropathy, and abnormal cell apoptosis [8]. Although various factors have been identified in the development of diabetic ulcers, the precise interactions between them remain unclear. As a result, there is

currently a lack of specific targets for interventions aimed at treating diabetic ulcers.

Research has demonstrated that diabetic wound healing is hindered by various factors, such as

insufficient neoangiogenesis, heightened oxidative stress, disproportionate inflammatory response, peripheral neuropathy, and abnormal apoptosis [9]. To improve the clinical healing process of diabetic

wounds, current approaches involve regulating the levels of fibroblast growth factors (FGFs) to accelerate the healing process [10]. While FGFs have shown promise in treating DFU wound healing, their

effectiveness is limited due to their short half-life and the need for repeated administrations [11]. Furthermore, the high and constant proteolytic environment of chronic wounds can degrade growth

factors quickly [12]. It remains unclear whether the long-term use of FGFs to treat diabetic ulcers could lead to systemic side effects. Thus, it is crucial to conduct thorough research to identify safe and

consistently effective factors that can aid in promoting diabetic wound healing. While some studies have identified potential factors [13], many of them are limited to cross-sectional or multi-omics analyses and

fail to provide a comprehensive view of the changes that occur in diabetic foot ulcers before treatment and after healing. Therefore, there is a need for more dynamic and longitudinal studies in this field.

This study aimed to analyze dynamic protein profile changes in normal hu-man-diabetic-pre-diabetic foot ulcer treatment-post-diabetic foot ulcer healing. Skin proteomics was used to screen for biomarkers that

affect diabetic foot ulcer healing [14]. Clinical case follow-up studies were conducted to confirm the feasibility of biomarkers as intervention targets. This paper aims to explore three main aspects related to

diabetic foot ulcer treatment. Firstly, it will showcase the dynamic changes in protein profiles from normal human to DFU patients, before and after treatment. Secondly, the study will conduct a fusion analysis of

serum and skin proteomics to identify potential proteins that promote the healing of DFU. Lastly, a clinical case follow-up study will be conducted to confirm the feasibility and mechanism of target

proteins as a treatment for DFU.

## Materials and Methods

1. Serum and skin proteomics analysis

1.1. Serum Preparation: Seven cases of age-matched normal subjects, five cases of diabetes mellitus,

and five cases of patients before treatment and correspondingly after healing of DFU were enrolled in the sample database of the First Affiliated Hospital of Fujian Medical University for serum proteomic analysis.

1.2. Tissue Preparation


<!-- Page 4 -->


Page 4/27

The sample bank of the First Affiliated Hospital of Fujian Medical University had collected six samples of

skin tissue from DFU biopsy, and six from control subjects. For DFU skin sampling: foot ulcers were cleaned with saline solution, and, after removing necrotic tissues, the ulcer marginal area was biopsied, a full layer of skin with a diameter of 5 mm was removed (Flow Chart 1). For control skin sampling: nondiabetic patients who had undergone foot surgery had a 5-mm diameter skin layer taken from the margin of the foot trauma. Sample processing: fresh tissue samples were flushed with PBS, quickly placed in

liquid nitrogen, and stored at -80°C.

1.3. Quantitative Protein Analysis

The tissue sample was grinded with liquid nitrogen into cell powder and then transferred to a 5mL centrifuge tube. After that, four volumes of lysis buffer (8M urea, 1% protease inhibitor cocktail, 3µM TSA and 50 mM NAM) was added to the cell powder, followed by sonication three times on ice using a high intensity ultrasonic processor (Scientz). The remaining debris was removed by centrifugation at 12,000 g at 4°C for 10 min. Finally, the supernatant was collected, and the protein concentration was determined

with BCA kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions. For di-gestion, the protein solution was reduced with 5 mM dithiothreitol for 60 min at 37°C and alkylated with 11 mM iodoacetamide for 45 min at room temperature in darkness. The protein sample was then diluted by adding 100 mM TEAB to urea concentration less than 2 M. Finally, trypsin was added at 1:50 trypsin-to-protein mass ratio for the first

digestion overnight and 1:100 trypsin-to-protein mass ratio for a second 4h digestion. Finally, the peptides were desalted by C18 SPE column. Tryptic peptides were first dissolved in 0.5 M TEAB. Each channel of peptide was labeled with their respective TMT reagent (based on manufacturer’s protocol, Thermo Scientific), and incubated for 2 hours at room temperature. Five microliters of each sample were pooled,

desalted, and analyzed by MS to check labeling efficiency. After labeling efficiency check, samples were quenched by adding 5% hydroxylamine. The pooled samples were then desalted with Strata X C18 SPE column (Phenomenex) and dried by vacuum centrifugation. The tryptic peptides were dissolved in solvent A (0.1% formic acid, 2% acetonitrile/in water), directly loaded onto a home-made re-versed-phase

analytical column (25cm length, 75/100 µm i.d.). Peptides were separated with a gradient from 6–22% solvent B (0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile) over 36 min, 22–32% in 16 min and climbing to 80% in 4 min then holding at 80% for the last 4 min, all at a constant flow rate of 500 nL/min on an EASY-nLC 1200 UPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific).

The separated peptides were analyzed in Q ExactiveTM HF-X (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with a nanoelectrospray ion source. The electrospray voltage applied was 2.1 kV. The full MS scan resolution was set to 120,000 for a scan range of 350–1600 m/z. Up to 20 most abundant precursors were then selected for further MS/MS analyses with 30 s dynamic exclusion. The HCD fragmentation was performed at a

normalized collision energy (NCE) of 28%. The fragments were detected in the Orbitrap at a resolution of 45,000. Fixed first mass was set as 100 m/z. Automatic gain control (AGC) target was set at 1E5, with an intensity threshold of 8.3E4 and a maximum injection time of 60 ms. The resulting MS/MS data were processed using Proteome Discoverer (v2.4.1.15). Tandem mass spectra were searched against the

human SwissProt database (20387 entries) concatenated with reverse decoy database. Trypsin/P was


<!-- Page 5 -->


Page 5/27

specified as cleavage enzyme allowing up to 2 missing cleavages. The mass tolerance for precursor ions was set as 10 ppm in the First search and 5 ppm in the Main search, and the mass tolerance for fragment ions was set as 0.02 Da. Carbamidomethyl on Cys was specified as a fixed modification. Acetylation on protein N-terminal, and oxidation on Met were specified as variable modifications. TMT-16plex

quantification was performed. FDR was adjusted to < 1% and minimum score for peptides was set to > 40.

1.4. Bioinformatics Analysis

Noise robust soft clustering of gene expression time-course data was implemented using the fuzzy C- Means algorithm in the Mfuzz package. The following parameters were set: The number of clusters k is set to 5; the degree of clustering fuzziness m is set to 2. This method may assign genes into several clusters according to the expression pattern of DEGs. Then, clusters with significant change tendency

were screened for further analysis. Gene ontology annotation terms and KEGG pathways were enriched using the online tool DAVID (version 6.8, https://david-d.ncifcrf.gov/), and the significant results were selected with P value < 0.05 and count ≥ 2. Then, differential proteins were uploaded to STRING (https://string-db.org/) to predict and construct PPI networks with a confidence level of > 0.4 (41, 42). The

node degree of proteins analyzed by STRING was used for ranking. Cytoscape was used to visualize the network. Nodes represent genes, and edges represent connections between genes. Genes were ranked by size according to the betweenness centrality (BC) score analyzed by the CytoNCA plugin. The cytoHubba plugin was used to rank genes by depth of the color corresponding to the weighted score based upon

maximal clique centrality (MCC) algorithms.

2.Clinical Case Studies

2.1. Study Population

We enrolled in the study 82 T2DM patients with diabetic foot ulcers, consisting of 53 males and 29 females and with mean age of 65.9 ± 10.2 years. Patients with diabetic foot ulcers were classified into five groups using the Wagner grading criteria: grade 1 (20 cases), grade 2 (26 cases), grade 3 (14 cases),

grade 4 (20 cases), and grade 5 (2 cases, not included in the post statistical analysis). In addition, we enrolled 240 age-matched patients with T2DM but without complication (141 males and 99 females) with mean age of 65.3 ± 9.3 years, and 160 age-matched healthy individuals (92 males and 68 females) with mean age of 65.7 ± 4.8 years. Participants were recruited from the Endocrinology and Neurology Department at the First Affiliated Hospital of Fujian Medical University (FMU) between November 1, 2010,

and July 1, 2021. The study was approved by the ethics committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of FMU, MRCTA, and ECFAH of FMU [2018]215, and written informed consent was obtained from the patients. The inclusion and exclusion criteria for the cohort and the Wagner criteria are described in Supplement 1.

2.2. Clinical Measurements


<!-- Page 6 -->


Page 6/27

Information regarding patient demographic characteristics, disease duration, lifestyle, medical history, and drug use history was obtained from medical records. All patients underwent a neurological

examination and a physical examination which included height, weight, and blood pressure. Blood pressure was measured after 15 min rest. Body weight and height were measured with the patient barefoot and wearing light clothes. The body mass index (BMI) of each patient was calculated as BMI =

weight (kg)/height2 (m2).

2.3. Biochemical Indices

A venous blood sample was collected in the morning after eight hour overnight fast. After 8 h of overnight fasting the following factors were measured in all subjects: fasting plasma glucose (FPG), triglycerides (TG), total cholesterol (TC), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), serum creatinine concentration (SCr), βHBA, and the routine hematological and biochemical parameters. Glycated hemoglobin A1c

(HbA1c) levels were detected with high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC; VARIANTTM II; BIO- RAD Laboratories Inc., Hercules, CA, USA). A 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) was performed as well. Plasma glucose was measured by glucose oxidase method using the AU2700 analyzer (Olympus Corporation, Tokyo, Japan) and specific reagents. The urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) was

calculated as albumin concentration (mg/L) divided by creatinine concentration (g/L). The eGFR was calculated with the CKD-EPI creatinine Eq. (2009) that can be expressed as a single equation:141×min (SCr/κ,1)α × max(SCr/κ,1) − 1.209×0.993 Age [×1.018 if female] [×1.159 if black] where SCr is serum creatinine, κ is 0.7 for females and 0.9 for males, α is − 0.329 for females and − 0.411 for males, min is

the minimum of SCr/κ or 1, and max is the maximum of SCr/κ or 1 .

2.4. Evaluation Of Diabetic Complications

The Ankle Brachial Index (ABI) of both lower extremities was determined by measuring the systolic

pressure of the posterior tibial or anterior tibial artery and the brachial artery in the ankle to then calculate the ratio between the arterial pressure in the ankle and the brachial artery pressure. Patients were

monitored by diabetic foot peripheral neuropathy screening system and whether there was peripheral neuropathy was determined by combining the patient's symptoms and signs. Whether there was diabetic retinopathy (Diabetes retinopathy, DR) was determined with fundoscopy.

2.5. Follow-up Study

All patients underwent skin biopsy to exclude malignant lesions. Patients underwent standardized clinical treatment, including antimicrobial application, nutritional support, and antiseptic dressing changes for the wound. At the end of the follow-up period, among the diabetic patients: 27 cases had improved (5 of

which healed completely); 46 cases had not improved; 7 cases displayed ulcer progression and 2 cases resulted in amputation (Flow Chart 2).

3. Statistical Analysis


<!-- Page 7 -->


Page 7/27

All analyses were carried out using IBM SPSS software version 18.0 (IBM, Armonk, NY, USA). The Kolmogorov–Smirnov test was used to test whether a variable conformed to a normal distribution. Statistical results are presented as mean ± standard deviation, median (interquartile range) or proportions. Differences in the baseline characteristics among control, diabetic, and DFU groups were analyzed by ANOVA test and post-hoc least significant difference t‐test, Kruskal–Wallis test and Nemenyi post–hoc test, and the χ2–test and partitions of the χ2–test post–hoc test. One-way screening for

diabetic foot was analyzed using a binary logistic regression model, with results expressed as Odds Ratio (OR) with a 95% confidence interval (CI). Bivariate correlations were used to analyze the interrelationship of factors influencing diabetic foot prognosis. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

## Results

1. Dynamic proteomic analysis based on normal human-diabetic-diabetic foot ulcers before treatment and after healing

To study the changes in protein dynamics in vivo during the progression from healthy indi-viduals (HT) to diabetic patients (DM), diabetic foot ulcers (DMDFU), and eventually, to ulcer healing (DMDFUT), we conducted a quantitative proteomic analysis of serum samples from each group to identify patterns of variation in serum proteins across these populations. In comparison to the HT group, the DM group exhibited 68 upregulated and 60 downregulated differential proteins. Similarly, the DMDFU group showed

78 upregulated and 96 downregulated differential proteins when compared to the DM group. Finally, the DMDFUT group had 25 upregulated and 37 downregulated differential proteins when compared to the DMDFU group (Fig. 1A-C).

The results of the Mfuzz clustering analysis indicated that the protein expression in Cluster 1 was higher in the DMDFU group, but lower in the DMDFUT group when compared to the DMDFU group. Conversely, the protein expression in Cluster 4 was lower in the DMDFU group, but higher in the DMDFUT group when compared to the DMDFU group (Fig. 1D). The proteins of Cluster 1 were found to be enriched in protein activation cascade, immunoglobulin production, and complement activation through GO and KEGG

enrichment analysis. This was further supported by the involvement of signaling pathways such as complement and coagulation cascades and staphylococcus aureus infection(Fig. 1E,F). The proteins found in Cluster 4 were primarily associated with the regulation of endothelial cell migration, negative regulation of vasculature development, and angiogenesis (Fig. 1G). These proteins were mainly involved in ECM-receptor interaction, platelet activation, and focal adhesion signaling pathways (Fig. 1F). According to serum proteomics, the promotion of diabetic ulcer healing is related to neovascularization, whereas factors that impede the healing process are primarily associated with infection and immunity.

2. Cross-analysis of serum and skin proteomics

To identify skin tissue-specific target proteins, we conducted skin biopsies of both normal and diabetic foot ulcer wounds. This was done due to the weak tissue specificity of serum-derived proteins. The biopsied tissues were then subjected to quantitative skin proteomic analysis and cross-analyzed with


<!-- Page 8 -->


Page 8/27

corresponding normal and pretreatment diabetic foot ulcer serum proteomics. The Venn diagram revealed that there were 20 proteins that were upregulated and 41 proteins that were downregulated in both groups (Fig. 2A-B). Upon further analysis, the top hub genes were identified, indicating a high degree of interrelatedness among these genes. The significant nodes identified by the cytoHubba plug-in in

Cytoscape (Fig. 2C). The top three hub genes, as determined by the MCC method, were APOA1, LPA, and APOA2 (Fig. 2D). These proteins are known to play a crucial role in lipid metabolism.

3. APOA1 levels decreased in patients with DFU

To validate the target proteins identified through proteomic screening, we conducted clinical case controls to analyze the correlation between these proteins and diabetic foot ulcers. As a hub protein of TOP1, we selected the APOA1 protein for validation of the target protein. The study found that compared to the control and diabetic groups, the DFU group had increased coagulation-related indexes such as PLT, FIB,

and D-2polymer (P < 0.05), as well as increased inflammatory response indexes such as WBC, NEU, NLR, and CRP (P < 0.05). Additionally, the diabetic foot ulcer group had decreased levels of ALB, Hb, TBIL, and APOA1 (all P < 0.05). However, no significant differences were observed in age and sex parameters (Table 1).

4. APOA1 was negatively correlated with the Wagner classification of DFU

To investigate the correlation between APOA1 and DFU, we categorized APOA1 into four levels based on four percentiles: the 25th percentile (APOA1 ≤ 0.97 mmol/L), 25-50th percentile (0.97 < APOA1 ≤ 1.14 mmol/L), 50-75th percentile (1.14 < APOA1 ≤ 1.26 mmol/L), and > 75th percentile (APOA1 > 1.26


<!-- Page 11 -->


Page 11/27

mmol/L). We conducted several logistic regression analyses and observed a negative correlation between APOA1, APOA1/APOB, ALB, and TBIL levels and diabetic foot ulcers (Fig. 3A). On the other hand, FIB, NLR, WBC, NEU, HbA1c, and DPN were positively correlated with diabetic foot ulcers (Fig. 3A). To investigate the potential independent association between APOA1 and diabetic foot ulcers, we created two models: The study found that APOA1 was negatively associated with diabetic foot ulcers in Model #1 after adjusting for neuropathy and bilateral ABI (OR = 0.528, 95%CI = 0.320–0.868, P = 0.012; Fig. 3B). However, in Model #2, after adjusting for the coagulation index (FIB) and inflammation index (NLR, WBC,

NEU), no significant relationship between APOA1 and diabetic foot ulcers was detected (OR = 0.791, 95%CI = 0.575–1.089, P = 0.151; Fig. 3C).

To avoid biases, only two patients classified as Wagner class 5 were included in this part of the study to confirm the effects of APOA1 on the severity of diabetic foot ulcers. Trend analysis revealed that the APOA1 level decreased with an increase in the Wagner grade(Fig. 4A). The results of Spearman correlation analysis indicate that APOA1 and APOA1/APOB have a negative correlation with the Wagner grade of diabetic foot ulcers, with correlation coefficients of -0.347 and − 0.257 respectively, and a pvalue < 0.05. On the other hand, FIB, PLT, NEU, and WBC have a positive correlation with the Wagner grade

of diabetic foot ulcers, with correlation coefficients of 0.438, 0.228, 0.268, and 0.248 respectively, and a pvalue < 0.05 (Fig. 4B).

5. APOA1 levels increased after improvement of treated DFU

To investigate the correlation between APOA1 and DFU, we categorized APOA1 into four levers. Our study found that APOA1 is negatively correlated with the severity of ulcers in diabetic patients, serving as an independent factor. To establish a causal relationship between APOA1 and diabetic foot ulcers’ prognosis, we monitored patients for 3–6 months after ulcer treatment. We defined improvement as a

decrease of one or more grades in Wagner's classification or a full wound healing. In our study, we found that out of the total 82 cases observed, 27 cases showed improvement while 46 cases did not show any improvement. However, 7 cases presented ulcer progression with Wagner grade ≥ 1, and 2 cases resulted in amputations (Fig. 5A). Among the 27 improved cases, 5 cases were completely healed, 18 cases decreased by one grade in Wagner's classification, and 4 cases decreased by more than one grade in Wagner's classification (Fig. 5B). Our study compared APOA1 levels during pre-treatment and found that patients with diabetic foot ulcers who improved with treatment had recovered levels of APOA1. Additionally, patients with ulcer progression showed further downregulation of APOA1 levels, while

patients who showed no change in ulcer conditions did not exhibit a statistical difference in APOA1 levels (Fig. 5C). These findings indicate that APOA1 may function as a protective factor for DFU.

6. APOA1 is involved in the healing of diabetic foot ulcers by affecting coagulation, inflammation, angiogenesis, and wound repair

Prior research has indicated that APOA1 may serve as a safeguard against diabetic foot ulcers. In order to delve deeper into the specific ways in which APOA1 impacts the healing of these ulcers, we conducted a proteomic analysis on the skin surrounding diabetic foot ulcer margins, with normal skin serving as our


<!-- Page 12 -->


Page 12/27

control. Through this analysis, we were able to identify a total of 1290 differentially expressed proteins (DEPs). To investigate the functions associated with DEPs, we obtained four sets of genes from the 'GSEA' database that are related to inflammation, coagulation, angiogenesis, and poor wound healing: "GOBP_ACUTE_INFLAMMATORY_RESPONSE" (Figure S1A), "HALLMARK_COAGULATION" (Figure S1B), "ANGIOGENESIS" (Figure S1C) and "HP_POOR_WOUND_HEALING" (Figure S1D). We then conducted PPI

analysis on these gene sets with DEPs to filter out related proteins.

This study identified a total of 16 DEPs involved in inflammation-related processes (Fig. 6A), 32 DEPs involved in coagulation-related processes (Fig. 6B), 7 DEPs in angiogenesis-related processes (Fig. 6C), and 4 DEPs in wound re-pair-related processes (Fig. 6D). Among the DEPs, the top ten up-regulated proteins were PRTN3, S100A2, LCE3D, S100A8, S100A9, PRIM2, DEFA1, ELANE, S100A7, and S100PBP (Fig. 6E). Conversely, the top ten down-regulated proteins were LUM, FABP7, HBB, HBA1, OGN, PRELP,

PLAC9, APOA1, KRT2, CLEC3B (Fig. 6E). The ten most significant DEPs between up-regulated and downregulated DEPs were found to be involved in coagulation-related processes such as APOA1, and

inflammation-related processes such as S100A8 and ELANE. These wound healing-related genes are primarily involved in cellular and intracellular processes, as well as developmental processes, biological

regulation, response to stimulus, localization, and binding.

To investigate the interaction relationships between differential proteins within each gene set (inflammation, coagulation, angiogenesis, and poor wound healing), we conducted a mutual analysis of

the differential protein sets associated with each set and extracted the interactions with a confidence score of 0.7 (high confidence) using the STRING (v.11.5) database (Fig. 6F). The interactions were

imported into the Cytoscape software, and the top ten hub node genes were screened with Cytohubba: APOA1, Apolipoprotein A-II (APOA2), Apolipoprotein C-I(APOC1), Apolipoprotein C-II (APOC2),

Apolipoprotein C-III (APOC3), Haptoglobin (HP), Clusterin(CLU), Serum amyloid A-1 protein (SAA1), Haptoglobin-related protein(HPR), and Serum amyloid A-4 protein (SAA4) were all down-regulated

proteins. APOA1 was most significantly down-regulated, being decreased 0.215 times (Fig. 6G),

suggesting that APOA1 is implicated in the healing of diabetic foot ulcers by affecting coagulation, inflammation, angiogenesis, and wound healing.

## Discussion

This study aimed to identify target proteins that promote diabetic wound healing by combining multitissue proteomic analysis and a clinical case follow-up study. We conducted a dynamic proteomic

analysis to analyze the function of proteins that affect the prognosis of DFU. We then screened target proteins in skin proteomic analysis and confirmed the correlation with the severity and prognosis of

APOA1 in DFU through a clinical case study. In conclusion, our analysis shows that APOA1 may affect local coagulation, inflammation, angiogenesis, and wound healing in DFU.

Proteomics has shown promise in the diagnosis and treatment of DFU [14–16]. However, current studies tend to focus on individual mechanisms related to inflammation, coagulation, extracellular matrix, or


<!-- Page 13 -->


Page 13/27

angiogenesis, rather than exploring the combination of these pathways [17–20]. Additionally, most

studies are limited to a single tissue, such as serum or skin, and fail to capture the dynamic changes that occur during the transition from normal to diabetic to DFU to wound healing. In this study, we utilized

dynamic serum proteomics and skin proteomic analysis of patients to identify proteins that may improve the prognosis of diabetic foot ulcers. Our findings shed light on potential targets for treatment that have

not been previously reported.

To validate the correlation between target proteins and DFU, we expanded our clinical samples. After

adjusting for age and gender, we observed a gradual increase in coagulation-related and inflammatory

response indicators from the control population to the diabetic population, and finally to the diabetic population with foot ulcers. Conversely, nutritional and antioxidant indicators decreased in the same

pattern. Our findings support previous studies suggesting that DFU patients with impaired healing are closely linked to chronic inflammation [21–23] and coagulation abnormalities [24]. The antifibrinolytic

system can cause hemodynamic disorders [25] in the feet of diabetic patients, exacerbating endothelial dysfunctions in DFU [26]. Our study revealed a reduction in APOA1 levels among patients diagnosed with

DFU. Additionally, we observed a negative correlation between APOA1 and DFU, indicating that APOA1 is

a significant factor that is negatively associated with the development of DFU. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the relationship between APOA1 and DFU is not influenced by ABI and DPN but is affected

by coagulation index and inflammation index. Our findings indicate that APOA1 may play a role in the interaction between inflammation and coagulation. This is supported by previous research, such as the

study conducted by Nanda R et al., which suggests that APOA1 has the potential to predict DFU [27, 28]. However, it is important to note that their study was cross-sectional in nature and further prospective

follow-up studies are needed to confirm the use of APOA1 as a reliable biomarker for DFU.

To investigate the role of APOA1 in the severity and prognosis of DFU, we conducted trend analysis and

Spearman correlation analysis. Our findings indicate that APOA1 is negatively correlated with Wagner

grade, suggesting that APOA1 has the potential to predict the severity of DFU. To establish a causal relationship between APOA1 and DFU, we conducted a follow-up study on patients with diabetic foot

ulcers. We compared their serum APOA1 levels before and after 3–6 months of treatment and observed that APOA1 levels increased in patients who showed improvement in their ulcers, while there was no

significant change in the levels of APOA1 in patients who did not show any improvement. Our findings provide additional evidence that APOA1 serves as a protective factor against DFU, and may also play a

role in predicting the severity and prognosis of ulcers. While clinical evidence is currently lacking

regarding the promotion of healing in diabetic foot ulcers by APOA1, previous studies in other areas suggest that this hypothesis may hold true [29]. The study showed that APOA1 can modify wound

healing kinetics and promote rapid healing of scratched wounds [30, 31]. Another study revealed that APOA1 mimetic peptide D-4F enhances carotid artery endothelial proliferation and migration, leading to

improved wound healing in mice [32]. These findings provide additional evidence supporting APOA1's capacity to facilitate wound healing. Our research contributes to the existing literature and reinforces the

possible role of APOA1 in predicting ulcer severity and prognosis.


<!-- Page 14 -->


Page 14/27

To investigate the potential mechanism by which APOA1 benefits diabetic foot ulcers, we conducted a skin proteomics analysis and obtained four relevant gene sets (inflammation, coagulation, angiogenesis,

and poor wound healing related gene sets) from the 'GSEA' database that is involved in wound healing. The subsequent protein interaction analysis showed that APOA1 was the key protein of DFU. It is believed

that APOA1 may affect local coagulation, inflammation, angiogenesis, and wound repair [33–35]. Although the mechanism of APOA1 participating in DFU is still unclear, its effects on coagulation,

inflammation, and angiogenesis have been confirmed in non-diabetes patients. In a study conducted by

Pan B. et al., it was discovered that APOA1 can prevent inflammation in endothelial cells by increasing the expression of the mem-brane-linked protein A1 and inhibiting the activation of phospholipase A2 [36].

Similarly, Wacker B. K. et al. demonstrated that the induction of high APOA1 expression (HDAdApoAI) can lead to a decrease in macrophage content and promote the rapid regression of small and medium-sized

atherosclerosis [37]. Other studies have demonstrated that APOA1 can decrease thrombosis by enhancing the endothelial barrier's integrity, increasing the degradation of procoagulant extracellular

histones, and inhibiting the activity of vascular hemophilia factor (vWf) [38]. APOA1 mimetic peptides

have been shown to promote cholesterol efflux and improve pathological processes in various model animals. Furthermore, these peptides have pleiotropic effects, including anti-inflammatory, antioxidant,

antithrombotic, and lipogenic effects [39, 40].

In this study, we utilized dynamic serum proteomics and skin proteomics to screen for target proteins that

affect diabetic foot ulcers. We then conducted clinical case studies to confirm the significance of these target proteins as a potential treatment for DFU. Additionally, we used bioinformatics analysis to

preliminarily elucidate the mechanism by which the target protein APOA1 affects ulcer healing. Our study has revealed that APOA1 can have a protective effect on diabetic foot ulcers by interacting with proteins

related to ulcer tissue coagulation, inflammation, angiogenesis, and wound repair. We have confirmed the

role of APOA1 in promoting the healing of DFU. One of the APOA1 candidate proteins was extracted from patients' self-serum and infused back into the wounds to promote the healing of ulcers.

Limitations: Firstly, the study only included two patients classified as Wagner grade 5 and did not include any Wagner grade 5 patients in the late statistical analysis. As a result, the findings of this study cannot

be considered representative of patients with severe diabetic foot ulcers. Secondly, the number of cases is low. In order to further confirm the role of target proteins in promoting the healing of diabetic foot ulcers,

we suggest expanding the clinical case-control study. Thirdly, our research is limited to clinical and

human subject analysis. Therefore, the effects of APOA1 on the local coagulation, inflammation, angiogenesis, and wound-healing mechanism of diabetes foot ulcers need to be further studied through

animal experiments.
